questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the primary function of the electrocardiogram (ECG)?
options: It records the mechanical contraction of the ventricular myocardium directly
It records the heart's electrical activity and displays it as a waveform tracing
It measures blood flow velocity across the cardiac valves
It directly images chamber dimensions in real time
questions.explanation: The ECG detects and graphically records the heart's electrical activity as a waveform tracing. It does not record contraction itself (that is mechanical), measure flow (Doppler), or image structures (echo).
tags: ECG Basics and Why the ECG Matters in Echocardiography

questions.stem: The fundamental relationship between electrical and mechanical events in the heart is that:
options: Mechanical contraction occurs after the electrical activation that triggers it
Mechanical contraction occurs before any electrical activity
Electrical activity and contraction occur simultaneously at the same instant
Contraction is independent of electrical stimulation in healthy myocardium
questions.explanation: Electrical depolarization of myocardial cells triggers contraction, so mechanical events follow electrical events. This relationship is the entire basis for using the ECG to time echo measurements.
tags: ECG Basics and Why the ECG Matters in Echocardiography

questions.stem: The ECG is valuable during echocardiographic examination primarily because it:
options: Replaces the need for Doppler assessment
Images the chamber walls more clearly than ultrasound
Reflects the timing of the cardiac cycle in real time
questions.explanation: The ECG displays the timing of depolarization and repolarization, allowing the sonographer to know where the heart is within the cardiac cycle during image acquisition. It provides real-time information that guides clinical and echo assessment.
tags: ECG Basics and Why the ECG Matters in Echocardiography

questions.stem: The ECG is widely used in clinical practice largely because it is:
options: Non-invasive and provides real-time cardiac information
Limited to use during cardiac surgery only
questions.explanation: The ECG is non-invasive, painless, inexpensive, and provides real-time information about the heart's electrical activity, making it suitable for continuous monitoring during examinations.
tags: ECG Basics and Why the ECG Matters in Echocardiography

questions.stem: The deflections seen on an ECG tracing directly represent:
options: The physical movement of the valve leaflets
The volume of blood ejected with each beat
The timing of myocardial depolarization and repolarization
The pressure changes within the cardiac chambers
questions.explanation: Each ECG deflection corresponds to the depolarization or repolarization of specific heart muscle and its timing. Pressure, volume, and valve motion are mechanical events assessed by other means.
tags: ECG Basics and Why the ECG Matters in Echocardiography

questions.stem: A complete P–QRS–T tracing on the ECG represents:
options: Only the electrical activity of the ventricles
One full minute of cardiac rhythm
questions.explanation: One P–QRS–T sequence reflects the electrical events of a single cardiac cycle, from atrial depolarization through ventricular repolarization.
tags: ECG Basics and Why the ECG Matters in Echocardiography

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about electrical activity and contraction is TRUE?
options: Electrical activity follows contraction by a fixed delay
Electrical and mechanical events are unrelated
questions.explanation: Electrical activation always precedes the mechanical contraction it triggers. The brief delay between the two allows echo measurements to be timed from the ECG.
tags: ECG Basics and Why the ECG Matters in Echocardiography

questions.stem: Because the ECG reflects the timing of the cardiac cycle, the sonographer can use it to:
options: Measure the thickness of the pericardium
Identify when systole and diastole occur during imaging
questions.explanation: The ECG marks the phases of the cardiac cycle, so systole and diastole can be identified on the tracing and correlated with the ultrasound image. Hemodynamic and structural assessments require echocardiographic techniques.
tags: ECG Basics and Why the ECG Matters in Echocardiography

questions.stem: In a combined ECG–echocardiographic study, which modality provides the assessment of blood flow and hemodynamics?
questions.explanation: Echo evaluates blood flow and hemodynamics via Doppler; the ECG contributes only electrical timing. The two modalities provide complementary cardiac information.
tags: ECG Basics and Why the ECG Matters in Echocardiography

questions.stem: ECG gating is used during echocardiography primarily to:
options: Synchronize image acquisition with the cardiac cycle
Increase the frame rate of the transducer
Measure the patient's blood pressure continuously
questions.explanation: Gating uses the ECG to synchronize image acquisition to specific phases of the cardiac cycle, identifying systole and diastole for consistent, reproducible measurements.
tags: ECG Basics and Why the ECG Matters in Echocardiography

questions.stem: Which of the following assessments is NOT provided by the ECG?
questions.explanation: Valve motion and chamber size are structural/mechanical findings evaluated by echocardiography. The ECG supplies electrical information such as rhythm, rate, and timing.
tags: ECG Basics and Why the ECG Matters in Echocardiography

questions.stem: The ECG waveform is best described as a graphic representation of:
options: The summed electrical activity of the heart detected at the body surface
Mechanical shortening of individual myocardial fibers
questions.explanation: Surface electrodes detect the summed electrical activity of countless depolarizing and repolarizing cells, which is plotted over time as the ECG waveform.
tags: ECG Basics and Why the ECG Matters in Echocardiography

questions.stem: Depolarization of ventricular myocardial cells normally results in:
options: Mechanical contraction of the ventricular muscle
Passive relaxation of the atria only
questions.explanation: Depolarization is the electrical trigger for contraction; when the ventricles depolarize (QRS), ventricular systolic contraction follows. Filling and valve motions are consequences of the pressure changes that follow.
tags: ECG Basics and Why the ECG Matters in Echocardiography

questions.stem: If a patient's ECG shows no organized electrical activity, the expected mechanical result is:
options: Forceful coordinated contraction of all chambers
questions.explanation: Electrical activity triggers contraction; without organized electrical activation, coordinated mechanical contraction cannot occur. This underlies the importance of the ECG in assessing cardiac function.
tags: ECG Basics and Why the ECG Matters in Echocardiography

questions.stem: The timing information displayed on the ECG is clinically useful because it allows:
options: Identification of systolic and diastolic phases for echo measurements
questions.explanation: By marking depolarization and repolarization events, the ECG lets the sonographer identify systole and diastole, which supports accurate, standardized echocardiographic measurements.
tags: ECG Basics and Why the ECG Matters in Echocardiography

questions.stem: The ECG's ability to provide real-time cardiac information is important because it:
options: Guides clinical and echocardiographic assessment as events occur
Stores data for analysis days later
Eliminates the need for patient history
Only functions after image acquisition is complete
questions.explanation: The ECG displays the heart's electrical events continuously and in real time, guiding both clinical judgment and the timing of the echocardiographic examination as it happens.
tags: ECG Basics and Why the ECG Matters in Echocardiography

questions.stem: Before an echocardiographic image can be interpreted in relation to the cardiac cycle, the sonographer must first understand:
options: The physics of ultrasound attenuation only
The surgical history of the patient
The electrical events of the cardiac cycle and their ECG timing
questions.explanation: Because mechanical function follows electrical activation, interpreting images against the cardiac cycle requires knowledge of the ECG waveforms and the timing they represent.
tags: ECG Basics and Why the ECG Matters in Echocardiography

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly pairs a modality with its primary assessment?
options: ECG — chamber size and valve motion
ECG — electrical activity and rhythm; echo — structure, motion, and flow
Both modalities measure only blood pressure
questions.explanation: The ECG records electrical activity and rhythm, while echocardiography evaluates chambers, valves, motion, and blood flow. Confusing the two roles is a common distractor on credentialing exams.
tags: ECG Basics and Why the ECG Matters in Echocardiography

questions.stem: The organized electrical impulse that spreads through both atria is recorded on the surface ECG as the:
questions.explanation: Atrial depolarization, initiated by the SA node and spreading through both atria, produces the P wave. Ventricular events produce the QRS and T wave.
tags: ECG Basics and Why the ECG Matters in Echocardiography

questions.stem: Why should the sonographer monitor the ECG tracing throughout the entire echocardiographic examination?
options: Because the rhythm affects image acquisition, event timing, and measurement reproducibility
Because the ECG can substitute for the Doppler assessment
Because the ECG confirms the transducer is positioned correctly
Because the ECG measures the acoustic window quality
questions.explanation: The rhythm determines how regularly the heart cycles, which directly influences image acquisition, Doppler timing, and the reproducibility of measurements. Continuous ECG monitoring is standard sonographer practice. ---
tags: ECG versus Echocardiography — Electrical and Mechanical Events

questions.stem: The ECG is best characterized as a recording of:
questions.explanation: The ECG records the heart's electrical activity and displays depolarization and repolarization timing as a rhythm tracing. Mechanical parameters belong to echocardiography.
tags: ECG versus Echocardiography — Electrical and Mechanical Events

questions.stem: Echocardiography contributes which of the following assessments that the ECG cannot?
options: Chamber sizes, valve function, wall motion, and blood flow
questions.explanation: Echo directly evaluates structure and function: chambers, valves, wall motion, and Doppler flow. Intervals and rhythm are ECG parameters, making them unsuitable distractors.
tags: ECG versus Echocardiography — Electrical and Mechanical Events

questions.stem: Depolarization of a myocardial cell refers to:
options: Return of the cell to its resting charged state
The electrical activation of the cell that triggers contraction
Passive blood flow into the chamber
questions.explanation: Depolarization is the rapid electrical change (ion movement) that activates the cell and triggers contraction. Repolarization is the return to the resting state.
tags: ECG versus Echocardiography — Electrical and Mechanical Events

questions.stem: Repolarization of the myocardium corresponds most closely with which mechanical event?
questions.explanation: Repolarization (the T wave) is the electrical recovery of the ventricles and is followed by ventricular relaxation, the beginning of diastole. The lecture emphasizes "repolarization followed by ventricular relaxation."
tags: ECG versus Echocardiography — Electrical and Mechanical Events

questions.stem: On a normal ECG, ventricular systole (contraction) begins shortly after the:
questions.explanation: The QRS represents ventricular depolarization, and the QRS complex precedes ventricular systole. The P wave relates to the atria; the T wave marks repolarization and relaxation.
tags: ECG versus Echocardiography — Electrical and Mechanical Events

questions.stem: The T wave corresponds to which combination of events?
options: Ventricular repolarization followed by ventricular relaxation
questions.explanation: The T wave represents ventricular repolarization; the myocardium then relaxes as diastole begins. This electrical-to-mechanical pairing is a core lecture concept.
tags: ECG versus Echocardiography — Electrical and Mechanical Events

questions.stem: A complete noninvasive cardiac assessment often combines the ECG and echocardiogram because:
options: The ECG and echo provide identical information
The ECG provides electrical timing while echo provides mechanical and structural information
Echo replaces the need for any electrical information
The ECG images the valves better than echo
questions.explanation: The two modalities are complementary: the ECG shows electrical events and rhythm; echo shows anatomy, motion, and flow. Neither alone gives the complete picture.
tags: ECG versus Echocardiography — Electrical and Mechanical Events

questions.stem: On the ECG, atrial depolarization is represented by the:
questions.explanation: The P wave is the first deflection of the cycle and represents atrial muscle depolarization as the impulse spreads from the SA node through both atria.
tags: ECG versus Echocardiography — Electrical and Mechanical Events

questions.stem: Atrial repolarization is not normally seen as a separate deflection on the ECG because it:
options: Occurs at the same time as ventricular depolarization and is hidden within the QRS
Does not occur in a normal heart
Is too weak to create any electrical signal
questions.explanation: Atrial repolarization occurs while the ventricles are depolarizing, so its small signal is buried within the much larger QRS complex and is not visible.
tags: ECG versus Echocardiography — Electrical and Mechanical Events

questions.stem: By the time the ventricles are in systole, the ECG has already displayed the:
questions.explanation: Electrical events precede mechanical ones; ventricular depolarization (QRS) must occur before ventricular contraction begins. The QRS is therefore visible before systole.
tags: ECG versus Echocardiography — Electrical and Mechanical Events

questions.stem: The period on the ECG immediately after the QRS complex and before the T wave corresponds to:
options: The plateau phase, with the ventricles in early sustained contraction
questions.explanation: The ST segment represents the interval when the ventricles are fully depolarized and in the plateau phase of the action potential, corresponding to early maintained ventricular contraction (systole).
tags: ECG versus Echocardiography — Electrical and Mechanical Events

questions.stem: If the conduction system fails to initiate and deliver an impulse to the ventricular myocardium, the ventricles will:
options: Fail to contract for that cycle until another pacemaker fires
Contract twice in the next cycle
Fill more rapidly and eject normally
questions.explanation: Electrical activation is required for contraction; without an impulse, no ventricular contraction occurs until a subsidiary pacemaker (junctional or ventricular) takes over.
tags: ECG versus Echocardiography — Electrical and Mechanical Events

questions.stem: Which of the following can the standard ECG NOT evaluate?
options: Blood flow velocities across the valves
questions.explanation: Flow velocities require Doppler echocardiography. Rate, intervals, and waveform durations are all ECG measurements.
tags: ECG versus Echocardiography — Electrical and Mechanical Events

questions.stem: Mechanical contraction follows electrical activation after a brief electromechanical delay; this fact explains why:
options: The ECG can be used to time mechanical events during echocardiography
The echo can measure the PR interval directly
Contraction occurs before the P wave
questions.explanation: Because contraction reliably follows its electrical trigger by a consistent brief delay, ECG events (like the QRS) serve as timing markers for mechanical events seen on echo.
tags: ECG versus Echocardiography — Electrical and Mechanical Events

questions.stem: The T wave on the ECG represents:
questions.explanation: The T wave is the waveform component representing ventricular repolarization, the electrical recovery that precedes ventricular relaxation.
tags: ECG versus Echocardiography — Electrical and Mechanical Events

questions.stem: Which ECG event most closely precedes the onset of ventricular systole?
questions.explanation: The QRS complex (ventricular depolarization) immediately precedes ventricular systole, as stated in the lecture: "QRS complex precedes ventricular systole."
tags: ECG versus Echocardiography — Electrical and Mechanical Events

questions.stem: Ventricular repolarization on the ECG is followed by:
options: Immediate atrial depolarization of the next beat
Ventricular relaxation and the start of diastole
questions.explanation: After the ventricles repolarize (T wave), the muscle relaxes and diastole begins, allowing ventricular filling. This mechanical sequence follows the electrical event.
tags: ECG versus Echocardiography — Electrical and Mechanical Events

questions.stem: Which statement about the information each modality displays is TRUE?
options: Echo displays depolarization timing; ECG displays valve excursion
The ECG displays depolarization and repolarization timing; echo evaluates chambers, valves, and motion
questions.explanation: The ECG's role is electrical timing; echo's role is structural and mechanical evaluation, including flow and hemodynamics. This division of labor is the key ECG-vs-echo concept.
tags: ECG versus Echocardiography — Electrical and Mechanical Events

questions.stem: The ECG feature most directly associated with the onset of ventricular mechanical contraction is the:
questions.explanation: Ventricular depolarization (QRS) is the electrical trigger that immediately precedes ventricular contraction. The P wave relates to atrial events; the segments are baseline intervals.
tags: ECG versus Echocardiography — Electrical and Mechanical Events

questions.stem: A patient has a completely normal ECG but echocardiography reveals a severely stenotic aortic valve. This combination demonstrates that:
options: A normal ECG does not exclude structural or mechanical cardiac disease
The ECG should have shown the stenosis as a wide QRS
Echo and ECG measure the same parameter
questions.explanation: The ECG records only electrical activity; a structurally diseased valve may produce a normal ECG. This is precisely why the two complementary modalities are both required. ---

questions.stem: The structure that functions as the normal pacemaker of the heart is the:
questions.explanation: The SA (sinoatrial) node initiates the organized electrical impulse that controls normal rhythm, making it the dominant pacemaker of the heart.

questions.stem: The primary function of the AV node in the conduction pathway is to:
options: Generate the fastest intrinsic rhythm in the heart
Briefly delay conduction before the impulse reaches the ventricles
questions.explanation: The AV node briefly delays ventricular conduction, allowing the atria to complete their contraction and empty into the ventricles before ventricular activation.

questions.stem: Which of the following lists the normal conduction pathway in correct sequence?
options: SA node → Purkinje fibers → AV node → bundle branches → Bundle of His
AV node → SA node → Purkinje fibers → Bundle of His → bundle branches
SA node → AV node → Bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers
Bundle of His → SA node → AV node → Purkinje fibers → bundle branches
questions.explanation: The impulse originates in the SA node, spreads through the atria to the AV node, is delayed, then passes through the Bundle of His, the bundle branches, and finally the Purkinje fibers, which stimulate coordinated contraction.

questions.stem: The right and left bundle branches function to:
options: Distribute the ventricular impulse to their respective ventricles
Delay the impulse at the AV junction
Pace the heart when the SA node is suppressed
questions.explanation: After the Bundle of His, the bundle branches distribute ventricular conduction to the right and left ventricles so both activate in an organized fashion.

questions.stem: The Purkinje fibers are responsible for:
options: Stimulating rapid, coordinated contraction of the ventricular myocardium
Initiating the heartbeat ahead of the SA node
questions.explanation: As the final links in the pathway, Purkinje fibers deliver the impulse to working ventricular cells, stimulating rapid, coordinated ventricular contraction.

questions.stem: The brief delay in conduction at the AV node corresponds to which ECG feature?
options: The PR interval (including the PR segment)
questions.explanation: The flat PR segment and the PR interval represent the time the impulse spends traversing the AV node and His–Purkinje system before ventricular depolarization begins.

questions.stem: The Bundle of His primarily serves to:
options: Conduct the impulse from the AV junction into the ventricular septum
questions.explanation: The Bundle of His is the conduction bridge that carries the impulse from the AV node through the fibrous skeleton into the ventricular septum, where the bundle branches take over.

questions.stem: If the SA node fails to fire, the next fastest pacemaker that normally takes over is the:
options: AV junction (AV node region), at about 40–60 bpm
questions.explanation: Intrinsic rates decrease down the conduction system: SA node 60–100, AV junction 40–60, ventricular Purkinje 20–40 bpm. The AV junction is therefore the first backup pacemaker.

questions.stem: The intrinsic discharge rate of ventricular (Purkinje) pacemakers is approximately:
questions.explanation: Ventricular escape pacemakers fire at only 20–40 bpm, which is why complete AV block below the His can produce profound bradycardia.

questions.stem: At rest in a healthy adult, the SA node typically initiates impulses at a rate of:
questions.explanation: The normal resting SA node rate of 60–100 bpm defines the normal heart rate range and corresponds to normal sinus rhythm.

questions.stem: The functional importance of the AV nodal delay is that it:
options: Allows the atria to complete contraction and finish filling the ventricles
Eliminates the need for atrial contraction
questions.explanation: The AV nodal delay gives atrial contraction time to complete ventricular filling before ventricular systole begins. Without this delay, filling would be incomplete.

questions.stem: After leaving the SA node, the impulse travels to the AV node:
options: Via the Purkinje network in the ventricles
questions.explanation: The impulse spreads through the atrial muscle (via internodal pathways), producing the P wave, before arriving at the AV node. The ventricular conduction structures are not involved yet.

questions.stem: Rapid, coordinated contraction of the entire ventricular muscle mass is achieved when the impulse reaches the:
questions.explanation: The Purkinje fibers conduct the impulse rapidly to the working ventricular cells, stimulating simultaneous, coordinated contraction of the ventricles.

questions.stem: The QRS complex of the ECG reflects conduction through which portion of the pathway?
options: The Bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers, and ventricular myocardium
questions.explanation: The QRS spans the time from the start of ventricular activation through the His–Purkinje system to full ventricular depolarization. Atrial and nodal events occur before the QRS.

questions.stem: If the AV node and surrounding junction fail as pacemakers, the expected escape rhythm arises from ventricular pacemakers at approximately:
questions.explanation: Intrinsic rates fall progressively down the pathway (SA 60–100, AV junction 40–60, ventricular 20–40 bpm), so a ventricular escape rhythm is markedly slow.

questions.stem: In the normal heart, the only electrical connection between the atria and the ventricles is the:
options: AV node and Bundle of His (AV junction)
questions.explanation: The AV junction (AV node and Bundle of His) is the sole normal pathway for the impulse to cross from atria to ventricles; accessory pathways are abnormal.

questions.stem: Occlusion or disease affecting the right bundle branch would produce:
options: Delayed activation of the right ventricle and a widened QRS
questions.explanation: When a bundle branch is blocked, the affected ventricle is activated late via cell-to-cell spread, prolonging the QRS (bundle branch block) and causing dyssynchronous contraction.

questions.stem: The PR interval represents the conduction time from:
options: Onset of the QRS to the end of the T wave
End of the P wave to end of the QRS
Onset of atrial depolarization (P) to the onset of ventricular depolarization (QRS)
QRS onset to T wave onset
questions.explanation: The PR interval is measured from the beginning of the P wave to the beginning of the QRS, encompassing atrial depolarization plus the AV nodal delay.

questions.stem: At rest, the SA node discharges at 60–100 times per minute. This rate determines:
options: The width of the QRS complex
The duration of the QT interval
The voltage of the P wave
questions.explanation: Because the SA node is the dominant pacemaker, its firing rate sets the heart rate; the other structures have slower intrinsic rates and normally do not control rate.

questions.stem: Electrical activity spreads through both atria and produces the P wave; the impulse then arrives at the:
questions.explanation: After atrial activation, the impulse converges on the AV node, where it is briefly delayed before entering the ventricular conduction system. ---
tags: ECG Waveform Components — P Wave, QRS Complex, and T Wave

questions.stem: The P wave on the ECG represents:
questions.explanation: The P wave is the first waveform component and represents depolarization of the atrial muscle. The AV delay is represented by the PR segment, not the P wave itself.
tags: ECG Waveform Components — P Wave, QRS Complex, and T Wave

questions.stem: The QRS complex represents:
questions.explanation: The QRS complex is the record of ventricular muscle depolarization. Because the ventricles are the largest mass, this deflection is the largest on the tracing.
tags: ECG Waveform Components — P Wave, QRS Complex, and T Wave

questions.stem: The T wave represents:
questions.explanation: The T wave represents electrical recovery (repolarization) of the ventricles; it is followed by ventricular relaxation and diastole.
tags: ECG Waveform Components — P Wave, QRS Complex, and T Wave

questions.stem: Atrial repolarization does not appear as a distinct deflection on the ECG because:
options: It occurs during the TP segment when the tracing is flat
It is buried within the QRS complex during ventricular depolarization
It is identical to the T wave in timing
questions.explanation: Atrial repolarization coincides with ventricular depolarization; the larger QRS voltage overwhelms the small atrial recovery signal, hiding it within the complex.
tags: ECG Waveform Components — P Wave, QRS Complex, and T Wave

questions.stem: On a routine tracing, one P–QRS–T sequence reflects:
questions.explanation: "One tracing reflects one cardiac cycle" — the complete waveform sequence corresponds to a single cycle of atrial and ventricular electrical activity.
tags: ECG Waveform Components — P Wave, QRS Complex, and T Wave

questions.stem: Which of the following describes a normal P wave in lead II?
options: Small, upright, rounded, and less than 0.12 second in duration
Inverted and wider than the QRS
questions.explanation: A normal P wave is a small, smooth, upright deflection (in lead II) lasting less than 0.12 s. Notched or peaked P waves suggest atrial enlargement; the P wave is never wider than the QRS.
tags: ECG Waveform Components — P Wave, QRS Complex, and T Wave

questions.stem: On the ECG, the first negative deflection preceding the R wave is called the:
questions.explanation: In QRS nomenclature, a negative deflection before the R wave is a Q wave, the upward deflection is the R wave, and a negative deflection after the R wave is an S wave.
tags: ECG Waveform Components — P Wave, QRS Complex, and T Wave

questions.stem: The normal duration of the QRS complex in adults is:
questions.explanation: Rapid Purkinje conduction normally completes ventricular depolarization in 0.06–0.10 s. Durations of 0.12 s or greater are abnormal (e.g., bundle branch block).
tags: ECG Waveform Components — P Wave, QRS Complex, and T Wave

questions.stem: A QRS complex measuring 0.14 second suggests:
options: Abnormal ventricular conduction, such as bundle branch block or a ventricular origin
questions.explanation: A QRS wider than 0.12 s indicates abnormal, prolonged ventricular depolarization — classically bundle branch block, ventricular ectopy, or ventricular pacing. AV block widens the PR, not the QRS.
tags: ECG Waveform Components — P Wave, QRS Complex, and T Wave

questions.stem: A broad, notched (bifid) P wave in lead II is most suggestive of:
questions.explanation: Prolonged, notched atrial depolarization reflects an enlarged left atrium ("P mitrale") as seen in mitral valve disease — a finding relevant to the echocardiographer.
tags: ECG Waveform Components — P Wave, QRS Complex, and T Wave

questions.stem: A tall, peaked P wave in lead II is most suggestive of:
questions.explanation: Tall, peaked P waves ("P pulmonale") reflect right atrial enlargement, often associated with right-sided pressure or volume overload — a correlate assessable on echo.
tags: ECG Waveform Components — P Wave, QRS Complex, and T Wave

questions.stem: Deep, symmetric T wave inversion across multiple leads is most commonly associated with:
questions.explanation: T wave inversion reflects abnormal ventricular repolarization and is a classic sign of ischemia. It may also prompt echocardiographic evaluation for wall motion abnormalities.
tags: ECG Waveform Components — P Wave, QRS Complex, and T Wave

questions.stem: In a normal ECG, the ST segment appears:
questions.explanation: The ST segment is normally flat (isoelectric), representing the plateau period when all ventricular cells are depolarized. Elevation or depression indicates abnormal repolarization.
tags: ECG Waveform Components — P Wave, QRS Complex, and T Wave

questions.stem: Significant ST segment elevation in the leads over an anatomic region of the heart suggests:
options: A normal variant in all patients
questions.explanation: ST elevation is the hallmark of acute transmural myocardial injury. The regional lead distribution helps localize the infarct, correlating with regional wall motion abnormalities on echo.
tags: ECG Waveform Components — P Wave, QRS Complex, and T Wave

questions.stem: The junction between the end of the QRS complex and the beginning of the ST segment is called the:
questions.explanation: The J point marks where ventricular depolarization ends and repolarization's plateau (ST segment) begins; it is the reference point for measuring ST deviation.
tags: ECG Waveform Components — P Wave, QRS Complex, and T Wave

questions.stem: The small deflection that sometimes follows the T wave is the:
questions.explanation: The U wave is a small, low-amplitude deflection after the T wave, thought to represent late repolarization; it becomes prominent in hypokalemia and drug effects.
tags: ECG Waveform Components — P Wave, QRS Complex, and T Wave

questions.stem: The P wave represents which of the following?
options: Depolarization of the atrial muscle, not the firing of the SA node itself
The SA node's internal pacemaker potential
questions.explanation: The SA node's own discharge is too small to be recorded on the surface ECG; the P wave reflects the atrial muscle depolarization the SA node's impulse triggers.
tags: ECG Waveform Components — P Wave, QRS Complex, and T Wave

questions.stem: Ventricular depolarization takes longer on the ECG than atrial depolarization because:
options: The AV node slows ventricular conduction completely
The T wave overlaps the QRS
The ventricular muscle mass is much larger than the atrial mass
The bundle branches conduct more slowly than atrial tissue
questions.explanation: Depolarization time relates to muscle mass: the far larger ventricles require a longer interval (up to 0.10 s) than the small atria (~0.08–0.11 s), making the QRS the largest, widest normal deflection.
tags: ECG Waveform Components — P Wave, QRS Complex, and T Wave

questions.stem: An ECG tracing with no identifiable P waves and an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: In atrial fibrillation, organized atrial depolarization is replaced by chaotic fibrillatory activity (no P waves), and the AV node conducts impulses irregularly, producing an irregularly irregular rhythm.
tags: ECG Waveform Components — P Wave, QRS Complex, and T Wave

questions.stem: The QT interval represents:
options: The total duration of ventricular depolarization and repolarization
questions.explanation: Measured from QRS onset to the end of the T wave, the QT encompasses the entire electrical systole of the ventricles — depolarization plus repolarization. ---
tags: ECG Intervals and Measurements — PR, QRS, QT, and Grid Timing

questions.stem: The normal adult PR interval is:
questions.explanation: The PR interval normally spans 0.12–0.20 s (3–5 small boxes), reflecting physiologic AV nodal delay. Values outside this range suggest conduction abnormality.
tags: ECG Intervals and Measurements — PR, QRS, QT, and Grid Timing

questions.stem: On the tracing, the PR interval is measured from:
options: The peak of the P wave to the peak of the R wave
The end of the P wave to the end of the QRS
The beginning of the P wave to the end of the T wave
The beginning of the P wave to the beginning of the QRS complex
questions.explanation: Interval measurement convention starts at the onset of the first wave and ends at the onset of the next: P onset to QRS onset defines the PR interval.
tags: ECG Intervals and Measurements — PR, QRS, QT, and Grid Timing

questions.stem: A PR interval consistently greater than 0.20 second with a P wave before every QRS indicates:
questions.explanation: A uniformly prolonged PR (>0.20 s) with 1:1 AV conduction is first-degree AV block: every impulse is conducted, but slowly through the AV node.
tags: ECG Intervals and Measurements — PR, QRS, QT, and Grid Timing

questions.stem: A PR interval shorter than 0.12 second suggests:
options: Abnormally rapid AV conduction or an accessory pathway
questions.explanation: An abnormally short PR means the impulse bypassed or raced through the normal AV delay — as in a junctional rhythm or pre-excitation (accessory pathway) — rather than a delay.
tags: ECG Intervals and Measurements — PR, QRS, QT, and Grid Timing

questions.stem: A QRS complex is considered abnormally wide when its duration exceeds:
questions.explanation: Normal QRS duration is 0.06–0.10 s; 0.12 s (3 small boxes) is the accepted threshold for "wide," indicating abnormal ventricular activation such as BBB or ventricular ectopy.
tags: ECG Intervals and Measurements — PR, QRS, QT, and Grid Timing

questions.stem: The QT interval is measured from:
options: The onset of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave
The onset of the P wave to the onset of the QRS
The peak of the R wave to the peak of the T wave
The end of the T wave to the next P wave
questions.explanation: The QT spans ventricular depolarization through repolarization, so it is measured from QRS onset to the terminal end of the T wave.
tags: ECG Intervals and Measurements — PR, QRS, QT, and Grid Timing

questions.stem: A normal QT interval at a typical resting heart rate is approximately:
questions.explanation: The normal QT is roughly 0.36–0.44 s at common resting rates, but it shortens with tachycardia and lengthens with bradycardia, which is why rate correction is used.
tags: ECG Intervals and Measurements — PR, QRS, QT, and Grid Timing

questions.stem: The corrected QT interval (QTc) is necessary because:
options: The QT is unrelated to heart rate
The T wave cannot be measured
The QRS duration is always constant
The raw QT shortens as heart rate increases, so it must be adjusted for rate
questions.explanation: Because QT duration varies inversely with heart rate, formulas such as Bazett's (QTc = QT/√RR) correct the measured QT to a rate-independent value for interpretation.
tags: ECG Intervals and Measurements — PR, QRS, QT, and Grid Timing

questions.stem: A markedly prolonged QT interval is clinically important because it predisposes the patient to:
questions.explanation: Prolonged repolarization creates a vulnerable period during which early beats can trigger torsades de pointes, a life-threatening polymorphic VT.
tags: ECG Intervals and Measurements — PR, QRS, QT, and Grid Timing

questions.stem: At the standard ECG paper speed of 25 mm/second, one small horizontal box represents:
questions.explanation: At 25 mm/s, 1 mm = 0.04 s; each large box (5 mm) equals 0.20 s. These values are the basis of all ECG interval and rate calculations.
tags: ECG Intervals and Measurements — PR, QRS, QT, and Grid Timing

questions.stem: At a paper speed of 25 mm/second, one large box (5 small boxes) represents:
questions.explanation: Five small boxes of 0.04 s each total 0.20 s per large box. Five large boxes therefore equal 1.0 second, and 30 large boxes equal a 6-second strip.
tags: ECG Intervals and Measurements — PR, QRS, QT, and Grid Timing

questions.stem: With standard ECG voltage calibration, the vertical scale is set so that:
questions.explanation: Standard calibration is 10 mm = 1 mV; each vertical millimeter is 0.1 mV. This standardization allows waveform amplitudes to be compared across studies.
tags: ECG Intervals and Measurements — PR, QRS, QT, and Grid Timing

questions.stem: A PR interval that spans 4 small boxes on the tracing measures:
questions.explanation: 4 small boxes × 0.04 s = 0.16 s, comfortably within the normal 0.12–0.20 s range. Interval measurement by box counting is a core ECG skill.
tags: ECG Intervals and Measurements — PR, QRS, QT, and Grid Timing

questions.stem: A QRS complex spanning 2.5 small boxes measures:
questions.explanation: 2.5 × 0.04 s = 0.10 s, the upper limit of normal QRS duration. Time is counted in boxes, not millivolts — amplitude and duration use different scales.
tags: ECG Intervals and Measurements — PR, QRS, QT, and Grid Timing

questions.stem: An RR interval spanning 15 small boxes corresponds to:
questions.explanation: 15 small boxes × 0.04 s = 0.60 s between R waves. By the rate formula (60 ÷ 0.60), this corresponds to a heart rate of 100 bpm.
tags: ECG Intervals and Measurements — PR, QRS, QT, and Grid Timing

questions.stem: When measuring waveform amplitudes on the ECG, the reference baseline used is the:
questions.explanation: Deviations are measured from the isoelectric baseline — typically the flat TP segment between the end of the T wave and the next P wave — where no electrical activity is recorded.
tags: ECG Intervals and Measurements — PR, QRS, QT, and Grid Timing

questions.stem: If the ECG paper speed is increased to 50 mm/second, each small box then represents:
questions.explanation: Doubling the paper speed halves the time per millimeter: 1 mm = 0.02 s and one large box = 0.10 s. Reading rules must be adjusted accordingly.
tags: ECG Intervals and Measurements — PR, QRS, QT, and Grid Timing

questions.stem: A PR interval spanning 5 small boxes measures:
options: 0.20 second — the upper limit of normal
0.12 second — the lower limit of normal
questions.explanation: 5 × 0.04 s = 0.20 s, exactly the upper boundary of the normal PR range. Anything longer is first-degree AV block.
tags: ECG Intervals and Measurements — PR, QRS, QT, and Grid Timing

questions.stem: Standard ECG calibration can be verified by confirming that the calibration mark measures:
questions.explanation: The standard calibration pulse is 10 mm (1 mV) tall, confirming the vertical scale before waveform amplitudes are interpreted.
tags: ECG Intervals and Measurements — PR, QRS, QT, and Grid Timing

questions.stem: The ST segment is measured from:
options: P wave onset to QRS onset
QRS onset to T wave onset
The end of the QRS (J point) to the beginning of the T wave
The end of the T wave to the next P wave
questions.explanation: The ST segment lies between the end of ventricular depolarization (J point) and the start of repolarization (T wave onset); it is normally isoelectric. ---
tags: Heart Rate Calculation — the 300 Rule, 6-Second Rule, and Rate Boundaries

questions.stem: The "300 rule" for estimating heart rate on a regular ECG states that the rate equals:
options: The number of small boxes between R waves multiplied by 0.04
The number of QRS complexes in 3 seconds
300 divided by the number of large boxes between consecutive R waves
The number of P waves counted in 1 minute
questions.explanation: Because each large box is 0.20 s, dividing 300 by the number of large boxes between R waves gives the rate (e.g., 300 ÷ 4 = 75 bpm). This shortcut works only for regular rhythms.
tags: Heart Rate Calculation — the 300 Rule, 6-Second Rule, and Rate Boundaries

questions.stem: Using the 300 rule, a rhythm with 4 large boxes between consecutive R waves has a heart rate of:
questions.explanation: 300 ÷ 4 = 75 bpm. Cross-check: an RR of 0.80 s gives 60 ÷ 0.80 = 75 bpm, confirming the shortcut.
tags: Heart Rate Calculation — the 300 Rule, 6-Second Rule, and Rate Boundaries

questions.stem: A regular rhythm with an RR interval of 2 large boxes corresponds to a rate of:
questions.explanation: 300 ÷ 2 = 150 bpm. The shorter the RR interval, the faster the rate — a useful mental anchor for the 300-rule sequence (300, 150, 100, 75, 60, 50).
tags: Heart Rate Calculation — the 300 Rule, 6-Second Rule, and Rate Boundaries

questions.stem: On a regular tracing, R waves separated by 5 large boxes indicate a heart rate of:
questions.explanation: 300 ÷ 5 = 60 bpm. Five large boxes equal 1.0 second between beats, so one beat occurs each second.
tags: Heart Rate Calculation — the 300 Rule, 6-Second Rule, and Rate Boundaries

questions.stem: A regular rhythm in which consecutive R waves are 3 large boxes apart has a rate of:
questions.explanation: 300 ÷ 3 = 100 bpm, the upper boundary of the normal resting rate range.
tags: Heart Rate Calculation — the 300 Rule, 6-Second Rule, and Rate Boundaries

questions.stem: The 6-second rule for heart rate is performed by:
options: Measuring the QT interval and doubling it
Counting the QRS complexes in a 30-large-box (6-second) strip and multiplying by 10
Dividing 300 by the number of small boxes between P waves
questions.explanation: Counting QRS complexes in 6 seconds and multiplying by 10 gives beats per minute. Because it uses a window rather than a single interval, it remains valid for irregular rhythms.
tags: Heart Rate Calculation — the 300 Rule, 6-Second Rule, and Rate Boundaries

questions.stem: On a 6-second rhythm strip, 7 QRS complexes are counted. The heart rate is approximately:
questions.explanation: 7 complexes × 10 = 70 bpm. The 6-second rule gives an approximation (in multiples of 10) and is the preferred method for irregular rhythms.
tags: Heart Rate Calculation — the 300 Rule, 6-Second Rule, and Rate Boundaries

questions.stem: For an irregularly irregular rhythm, which rate method should the sonographer use?
options: The 1500 rule applied to one RR interval
questions.explanation: With irregular rhythms, no single RR interval represents the rate, so interval-based shortcuts (300 rule, 1500 rule) are inaccurate; the 6-second count over many beats is used instead.
tags: Heart Rate Calculation — the 300 Rule, 6-Second Rule, and Rate Boundaries

questions.stem: Counting the number of small boxes between two consecutive R waves and dividing that number into 1500 provides:
options: The most precise heart rate for a regular rhythm
questions.explanation: The 1500 rule uses the finest grid division (1 small box = 0.04 s; 1500 ÷ boxes = bpm), giving the most accurate single-beat rate — but only when the rhythm is regular.
tags: Heart Rate Calculation — the 300 Rule, 6-Second Rule, and Rate Boundaries

questions.stem: In a regular rhythm, 10 small boxes separate two R waves. The heart rate is:
questions.explanation: 1500 ÷ 10 = 150 bpm. Equivalently, 10 small boxes = 2 large boxes, and 300 ÷ 2 = 150 bpm.
tags: Heart Rate Calculation — the 300 Rule, 6-Second Rule, and Rate Boundaries

questions.stem: In an adult, tachycardia is defined as a resting heart rate greater than:
questions.explanation: Tachycardia is a rate above 100 bpm in adults; bradycardia is below 60 bpm. The 60–100 range brackets normal resting rates.
tags: Heart Rate Calculation — the 300 Rule, 6-Second Rule, and Rate Boundaries

questions.stem: In an adult, bradycardia is defined as a resting heart rate less than:
questions.explanation: A rate below 60 bpm is bradycardia. Note that well-trained individuals may have rates in the 50s at rest, so clinical significance is judged with symptoms and hemodynamics.
tags: Heart Rate Calculation — the 300 Rule, 6-Second Rule, and Rate Boundaries

questions.stem: A heart rate of 75 bpm corresponds to an RR interval of approximately:
questions.explanation: Rate = 60 ÷ RR, so RR = 60 ÷ 75 = 0.80 s (4 large boxes), matching the 300-rule answer of 300 ÷ 4 = 75 bpm.
tags: Heart Rate Calculation — the 300 Rule, 6-Second Rule, and Rate Boundaries

questions.stem: The heart rate range for normal sinus rhythm in an adult is:
questions.explanation: Normal sinus rhythm requires a SA node–driven rate of 60–100 bpm with regular rhythm and normal waveform sequence. Rates outside this range are sinus brady- or tachycardia.
tags: Heart Rate Calculation — the 300 Rule, 6-Second Rule, and Rate Boundaries

questions.stem: In a patient with a heart rate of 180 bpm, the echocardiographer should anticipate:
options: Markedly shortened diastole with reduced ventricular filling time
Widened QRS complexes as a direct rate effect
questions.explanation: Tachycardia shortens diastole disproportionately, reducing filling time. Rapid rates also complicate image acquisition and make Doppler interpretation more difficult.
tags: Heart Rate Calculation — the 300 Rule, 6-Second Rule, and Rate Boundaries

questions.stem: A 6-second strip shows 12 QRS complexes. The heart rate is approximately:
questions.explanation: 12 complexes × 10 = 120 bpm, which is tachycardia (>100 bpm in adults).
tags: Heart Rate Calculation — the 300 Rule, 6-Second Rule, and Rate Boundaries

questions.stem: The 300 rule gives inaccurate results when applied to atrial fibrillation because:
options: There are no R waves in AFib
The paper speed is always doubled
The RR intervals vary, so no single interval represents the rate
The T waves are too tall
questions.explanation: The 300 rule relies on one representative RR interval, which only exists when the rhythm is regular. Irregular rhythms require the 6-second counting method.
tags: Heart Rate Calculation — the 300 Rule, 6-Second Rule, and Rate Boundaries

questions.stem: A regular rhythm has an RR interval of 0.60 second. The heart rate is:
questions.explanation: 60 ÷ 0.60 = 100 bpm. Equivalently, 0.60 s equals 3 large boxes and 300 ÷ 3 = 100 bpm.
tags: Heart Rate Calculation — the 300 Rule, 6-Second Rule, and Rate Boundaries

questions.stem: A patient's ECG shows a regular rate of 40 bpm with normal P–QRS–T sequences. On echocardiography, this rate would be expected to produce:
options: Prolonged filling time with a risk of reduced cardiac output
questions.explanation: Bradycardia lengthens diastole and filling time, but may reduce cardiac output if the rate is too slow to compensate with stroke volume, as noted in the lecture.
tags: Heart Rate Calculation — the 300 Rule, 6-Second Rule, and Rate Boundaries

questions.stem: With a ventricular rate of 150 bpm, which phase of the cardiac cycle is shortened the most?
questions.explanation: As rate increases, diastole shortens far more than systole, reducing filling time — the key hemodynamic consequence of tachycardia for the echocardiographer. ---
tags: ECG Gating and Correlation of the ECG with Echo Events

questions.stem: The primary purpose of ECG gating during echocardiography is to:
options: Synchronize image acquisition with specific phases of the cardiac cycle
questions.explanation: Gating uses the ECG to trigger or tag image frames to known points in the cycle, enabling consistent identification of systole and diastole across beats and studies.
tags: ECG Gating and Correlation of the ECG with Echo Events

questions.stem: On the ECG, end-diastole (just before ventricular contraction) is conventionally identified at the:
questions.explanation: The onset of the QRS marks the end of ventricular filling (maximum ventricular volume) and the electrical trigger of systole — the standard end-diastolic reference for measurements.
tags: ECG Gating and Correlation of the ECG with Echo Events

questions.stem: End-systole on the ECG corresponds most closely with:
options: The onset of the P wave
The end of the T wave
The end of the PR segment
The peak of the R wave
questions.explanation: Ventricular repolarization (T wave) occurs just before relaxation begins, so the end of the T wave marks the smallest ventricular volume — end-systole — used for systolic measurements.
tags: ECG Gating and Correlation of the ECG with Echo Events

questions.stem: Chamber dimension measurements during echocardiography are most often obtained during:
options: End-diastole, at or just after the onset of the QRS
The TP segment of alternate beats
questions.explanation: End-diastole is the standard phase for chamber measurements (e.g., LV internal diameter, wall thickness) because it represents maximal, reproducible ventricular volume.
tags: ECG Gating and Correlation of the ECG with Echo Events

questions.stem: When reviewing a stored cine loop, the sonographer uses the ECG to:
options: Identify which frames correspond to each phase of the cardiac cycle
questions.explanation: Cine loops are tagged by ECG timing, so the reviewer can select end-diastolic or end-systolic frames for measurement and confirm that a full cycle was captured.
tags: ECG Gating and Correlation of the ECG with Echo Events

questions.stem: ECG gating improves echocardiographic measurements primarily by:
options: Improving the consistency and reproducibility of chamber measurements
Shortening the examination time by half
questions.explanation: Measuring every heart at the same phase of the cycle makes serial and inter-patient comparisons valid — the core reason gating is essential during routine examinations.
tags: ECG Gating and Correlation of the ECG with Echo Events

questions.stem: Accurate Doppler timing assessment during echocardiography depends on the ECG because:
options: Doppler cannot record without a QRS trigger
The ECG measures flow velocity directly
Spectral events must be correlated with cardiac timing
questions.explanation: Doppler waveforms (e.g., mitral inflow E and A waves, LVOT outflow) are interpreted relative to the ECG, which identifies where in the cycle each flow event occurs.
tags: ECG Gating and Correlation of the ECG with Echo Events

questions.stem: During M-mode imaging, the ECG assists by:
options: Replacing the need for a transducer
Providing a timing reference for correlating valve motion with the cardiac cycle
Adjusting the sweep speed of the paper automatically
questions.explanation: M-mode records one-dimensional motion over time, and the simultaneous ECG allows valve excursions (opening, closure) to be matched to their electrical events.
tags: ECG Gating and Correlation of the ECG with Echo Events

questions.stem: On an M-mode tracing of the aortic valve, aortic valve closure corresponds to:
options: The onset of the QRS complex
The end of the T wave
The onset of the P wave
The peak of the R wave
questions.explanation: Aortic valve closure ends ventricular ejection at end-systole, coinciding with the end of ventricular repolarization (end of the T wave) — a classic ECG–M-mode correlation.
tags: ECG Gating and Correlation of the ECG with Echo Events

questions.stem: Mitral valve opening in early diastole on M-mode corresponds most closely with which ECG timing?
options: Just after the end of the T wave
At the onset of the P wave
At the peak of the R wave
questions.explanation: After the T wave, the ventricles relax, LV pressure falls below LA pressure, and the mitral valve opens to begin rapid filling — shortly after the terminal T wave.
tags: ECG Gating and Correlation of the ECG with Echo Events

questions.stem: The onset of the QRS complex corresponds to which mechanical event?
options: The electrical trigger for the onset of ventricular contraction
questions.explanation: The QRS onset marks ventricular depolarization, the electrical event that immediately precedes and triggers ventricular systole.
tags: ECG Gating and Correlation of the ECG with Echo Events

questions.stem: If a patient's ECG tracing is unreliable during an examination, the sonographer may fall back on:
options: Estimating phases from the respiratory cycle
Timing from valve motion on M-mode (e.g., mitral/aortic valve events)
Using only the P wave when available
questions.explanation: Mechanical landmarks such as aortic valve closure and mitral valve opening on M-mode or Doppler can substitute for ECG timing, though measurements become less standardized.
tags: ECG Gating and Correlation of the ECG with Echo Events

questions.stem: During echocardiographic image acquisition, images are frozen:
options: Randomly, since phase does not matter
During specific cardiac phases identified by the ECG
questions.explanation: The ECG displayed continuously during imaging allows frames to be frozen at chosen phases (classically end-diastole and end-systole) for measurement.
tags: ECG Gating and Correlation of the ECG with Echo Events

questions.stem: Throughout a standard echocardiographic examination, the ECG tracing is:
options: Recorded only at the start of the study
Turned off during Doppler to reduce artifact
Recorded only at the end of the study
questions.explanation: Continuous ECG display is standard practice so every image and Doppler sample can be correlated with the cardiac cycle in real time.
tags: ECG Gating and Correlation of the ECG with Echo Events

questions.stem: In a patient with an irregular rhythm, the most appropriate measurement strategy is to:
options: Average measurements over several cardiac cycles
Measure only the beat with the tallest R wave
questions.explanation: Beat-to-beat variability makes single-beat measurements unrepresentative; averaging over several beats improves accuracy and reproducibility, per the lecture's sonographer guidance.
tags: ECG Gating and Correlation of the ECG with Echo Events

questions.stem: When interpreting a Doppler spectral tracing, flow events are timed by correlating them with:
questions.explanation: Doppler interpretation is linked with cardiac timing shown on the ECG, allowing events like valve opening and ejection onset to be identified precisely.
tags: ECG Gating and Correlation of the ECG with Echo Events

questions.stem: End-diastole is the preferred phase for measuring ventricular dimensions because at that moment:
options: Ventricular volume is maximal and filling is complete
questions.explanation: End-diastole represents the fully filled ventricle, providing a standardized, reproducible reference for chamber size and wall thickness.
tags: ECG Gating and Correlation of the ECG with Echo Events

questions.stem: On transmitral Doppler, the A wave (late filling) corresponds to which ECG event?
options: Atrial contraction, following the P wave
questions.explanation: The P wave triggers atrial contraction, which forces the late diastolic filling component (A wave). Loss of this relationship, as in atrial fibrillation, abolishes the A wave.
tags: ECG Gating and Correlation of the ECG with Echo Events

questions.stem: The R wave is typically chosen as the gating trigger point because it:
options: Is the longest interval on the tracing
Is tall, sharp, and easy to detect reliably on every beat
questions.explanation: The R wave's large amplitude and steep slope make it the most consistent, machine-detectable landmark, which is why R-wave triggering is the standard for ECG gating.
tags: ECG Gating and Correlation of the ECG with Echo Events

questions.stem: A properly gated cine loop in echocardiography typically displays:
options: One or more complete cardiac cycles, timed by the ECG from end-diastole to end-diastole
A full minute of continuous imaging
questions.explanation: Gated acquisition captures the cycle between successive R waves, ensuring the loop contains the complete systole and diastole needed for measurements and review. ---
tags: Normal Sinus Rhythm and Basic Rhythm Recognition

questions.stem: Which set of criteria defines normal sinus rhythm?
options: Regular rhythm, rate 60–100, one upright P wave before every QRS, normal PR and QRS
Irregular rhythm with absent P waves
questions.explanation: NSR requires SA node control: regular, evenly spaced beats at 60–100 bpm, one P wave for each QRS, a normal PR interval, and normal conduction through the physiological pathway.
tags: Normal Sinus Rhythm and Basic Rhythm Recognition

questions.stem: In normal sinus rhythm, each P wave is followed by:
questions.explanation: A 1:1 P-to-QRS relationship confirms that every atrial impulse is conducted to the ventricles — a defining feature of NSR. More or fewer QRS complexes than P waves indicates AV block or other arrhythmia.
tags: Normal Sinus Rhythm and Basic Rhythm Recognition

questions.stem: Regularity of a rhythm on the tracing is assessed by comparing:
options: The heights of consecutive T waves
The consistency of the RR (or PP) intervals across the strip
questions.explanation: A regular rhythm shows even spacing between successive beats; NSR "appears regular and evenly spaced." Varying RR intervals define an irregular rhythm.
tags: Normal Sinus Rhythm and Basic Rhythm Recognition

questions.stem: An ECG shows a perfectly regular rhythm at a rate of 110 bpm with one upright P wave preceding each QRS and a normal PR interval. The rhythm is:
questions.explanation: The rhythm is otherwise normal but exceeds 100 bpm, making it sinus tachycardia. NSR and sinus bradycardia require rates within 60–100 and below 60, respectively.
tags: Normal Sinus Rhythm and Basic Rhythm Recognition

questions.stem: A regular rhythm at 45 bpm with a P wave before every QRS and a normal PR interval is:
questions.explanation: The SA node still controls the rhythm (P before each QRS) but at a rate below 60 bpm — sinus bradycardia, which the lecture notes may reduce cardiac output.
tags: Normal Sinus Rhythm and Basic Rhythm Recognition

questions.stem: Lead II is most commonly used for the rhythm strip because:
options: It has the largest QRS amplitude in every patient
Atrial depolarization (P waves) is usually most clearly visible in it
questions.explanation: Lead II's axis parallels atrial depolarization, so P waves are upright and prominent, making it ideal for identifying rhythm and P–QRS relationships.
tags: Normal Sinus Rhythm and Basic Rhythm Recognition

questions.stem: A beat that occurs early and is preceded by an abnormal-looking P wave with a normal-duration QRS is a:
questions.explanation: An early beat arising in the atria shows a premature (often abnormal) P wave and conducts normally through the AV node, producing a narrow QRS. PVCs lack a preceding P wave and are wide.
tags: Normal Sinus Rhythm and Basic Rhythm Recognition

questions.stem: On the tracing, a premature ventricular contraction (PVC) is recognized by:
options: An early beat with a narrow QRS and a preceding P wave
A dropped QRS after a prolonged PR
An early, wide, bizarre QRS complex without a preceding P wave
A short PR with a delta wave
questions.explanation: PVCs originate from ventricular ectopic foci, bypassing the normal conduction system; the result is an early, wide (>0.12 s), abnormal QRS with no related P wave.
tags: Normal Sinus Rhythm and Basic Rhythm Recognition

questions.stem: The pause that commonly follows a PVC, during which the next normal beat is delayed, is termed a:
questions.explanation: Because the PVC usually does not reset the SA node, the next sinus P wave arrives on schedule but cannot conduct (the ventricles are refractory), producing a full compensatory pause.
tags: Normal Sinus Rhythm and Basic Rhythm Recognition

questions.stem: The beat immediately following a PVC often produces a larger stroke volume because:
options: The longer filling interval (and enhanced contractility) increases preload
The heart rate is faster on that beat
The atria fibrillate during the pause
questions.explanation: The post-PVC diastole is longer, so the ventricle fills more completely; by the Frank–Starling mechanism, the post-extrasystolic beat ejects a larger stroke volume, which can cause measurements to fluctuate.
tags: Normal Sinus Rhythm and Basic Rhythm Recognition

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the ECG appearance of atrial fibrillation?
options: Regular rhythm with sawtooth atrial waves
No organized P waves, chaotic fibrillatory baseline, and an irregularly irregular ventricular response
Regular rhythm with prolonged PR interval
questions.explanation: In atrial fibrillation, organized atrial contraction no longer occurs; chaotic atrial activity replaces P waves, and the AV node conducts impulses at random intervals, producing an irregular ventricular rhythm.
tags: Normal Sinus Rhythm and Basic Rhythm Recognition

questions.stem: Loss of the atrial kick in atrial fibrillation reduces ventricular filling by approximately:
options: 0% — the atria contribute nothing at any heart rate
questions.explanation: Atrial contraction contributes roughly the last 20–30% of ventricular filling. Its loss (as in AFib) reduces filling and is especially significant when diastolic function is impaired.
tags: Normal Sinus Rhythm and Basic Rhythm Recognition

questions.stem: The term "irregularly irregular" on palpation or ECG most specifically suggests:
questions.explanation: A completely random, unpredictable RR pattern with no organizing rhythm is characteristic of atrial fibrillation. Respiratory sinus arrhythmia varies in a regular, cyclic pattern instead.
tags: Normal Sinus Rhythm and Basic Rhythm Recognition

questions.stem: How does an irregular rhythm such as atrial fibrillation affect Doppler echocardiographic velocities?
options: It has no effect on Doppler measurements
It systematically raises all velocities by 50%
Velocities vary from beat to beat with the varying stroke volume and filling
It only affects velocities recorded during systole
questions.explanation: Variable RR intervals change diastolic filling times, so stroke volume and Doppler velocities (e.g., mitral inflow) fluctuate beat to beat, making measurements less reproducible.
tags: Normal Sinus Rhythm and Basic Rhythm Recognition

questions.stem: A perfectly regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 170 bpm in which P waves are not clearly seen (buried in the preceding T waves) suggests:
questions.explanation: A regular, narrow-complex tachycardia without visible P waves indicates a rhythm originating above the ventricles (AV node or atria) at a rate too fast for P waves to be distinct.
tags: Normal Sinus Rhythm and Basic Rhythm Recognition

questions.stem: The key ECG distinction between a PAC and a PVC is that the PAC has:
options: A preceding premature P wave and a normal-duration (narrow) QRS, while the PVC has no P wave and a wide, bizarre QRS
A wider QRS than the PVC
A longer pause than the PVC always
No effect on the following beat
questions.explanation: PACs arise above the ventricles and conduct through the normal pathway (narrow QRS with a premature P wave); PVCs arise in the ventricles and depolarize them abnormally (wide QRS, no P wave).
tags: Normal Sinus Rhythm and Basic Rhythm Recognition

questions.stem: An ECG with a regular rate of 88 bpm, one upright P wave before each QRS, a PR of 0.16 s, and a QRS of 0.08 s is:
questions.explanation: All criteria are met: regular rhythm, rate within 60–100, 1:1 P–QRS relationship, normal PR (0.12–0.20 s), and normal QRS (0.06–0.10 s).
tags: Normal Sinus Rhythm and Basic Rhythm Recognition

questions.stem: Sinus arrhythmia is best described as:
options: An irregular rhythm with absent P waves requiring cardioversion
A phasic variation in RR interval, usually with respiration, with every P wave still conducted
A regular rhythm faster than 100 bpm
A wide-complex rhythm originating in the ventricles
questions.explanation: In sinus arrhythmia the SA node rate varies (classically speeding with inspiration), so RR intervals cycle regularly, but it is a normal benign variant with intact P–QRS relationships.
tags: Normal Sinus Rhythm and Basic Rhythm Recognition

questions.stem: A QRS complex that is not preceded by a P wave suggests that the impulse originated:
options: Below the atria — in the AV junction or ventricles
questions.explanation: Beats without a preceding P wave arise at or below the AV junction (junctional or ventricular escape beats, PVCs, or junctional rhythms), since atrial depolarization did not initiate the beat.
tags: Normal Sinus Rhythm and Basic Rhythm Recognition

questions.stem: A patient in sinus rhythm has a constant PR interval of 0.28 second with every P wave conducted. This is:
questions.explanation: A uniformly prolonged PR (>0.20 s) with 1:1 conduction defines first-degree AV block — delayed AV conduction but no dropped beats. ---
tags: Rhythm Effects on Echocardiography — AFib, PVCs, Tachycardia, Bradycardia, and Bundle Branch Block

questions.stem: The dominant echocardiographic relevance of atrial fibrillation is that it produces:
options: Regular ventricular rhythm with enhanced atrial filling
An irregular ventricular rhythm with loss of organized atrial contraction
Widened QRS complexes from delayed ventricular activation
questions.explanation: AFib eliminates organized atrial contraction and produces an irregular ventricular response, so ventricular filling varies between cycles and Doppler velocities become inconsistent.
tags: Rhythm Effects on Echocardiography — AFib, PVCs, Tachycardia, Bradycardia, and Bundle Branch Block

questions.stem: On transmitral pulsed-wave Doppler in a patient with atrial fibrillation, the expected finding is:
options: Variable E wave velocities with absence of the A wave
Tall, consistent A waves with every beat
Normal E–A separation with uniform velocities
Absent E waves with preserved A waves
questions.explanation: Without organized atrial contraction, there is no atrial kick and therefore no A wave; the E wave amplitude varies with the random preceding RR intervals.
tags: Rhythm Effects on Echocardiography — AFib, PVCs, Tachycardia, Bradycardia, and Bundle Branch Block

questions.stem: To obtain representative measurements in atrial fibrillation, the sonographer should:
options: Measure a single beat immediately after a long pause
Measure only the shortest RR interval
Average measurements over multiple cardiac cycles
questions.explanation: Because filling times and stroke volumes vary beat to beat, averaging over several cycles is the standard strategy for improving accuracy and reproducibility in irregular rhythms.
tags: Rhythm Effects on Echocardiography — AFib, PVCs, Tachycardia, Bradycardia, and Bundle Branch Block

questions.stem: Premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) originate from:
questions.explanation: PVCs arise from an ectopic focus within the ventricular myocardium, depolarizing the ventricles outside the normal conduction pathway and producing a wide, abnormal QRS.
tags: Rhythm Effects on Echocardiography — AFib, PVCs, Tachycardia, Bradycardia, and Bundle Branch Block

questions.stem: The classic QRS morphology of a PVC is:
options: Narrow with a preceding P wave
Wide (≥0.12 s), bizarre, with no preceding P wave
questions.explanation: Because the impulse bypasses the Purkinje system and spreads cell-to-cell, ventricular depolarization is slow and abnormal, producing the wide, bizarre QRS described in the lecture.
tags: Rhythm Effects on Echocardiography — AFib, PVCs, Tachycardia, Bradycardia, and Bundle Branch Block

questions.stem: A PVC tends to reduce stroke volume for that beat because:
options: It always occurs after full filling
It originates above the AV node
The early contraction occurs before the ventricle has filled adequately
questions.explanation: The premature beat interrupts diastole, so filling is incomplete and the ejected volume is small. The following post-PVC beat, with its longer filling time, often ejects more.
tags: Rhythm Effects on Echocardiography — AFib, PVCs, Tachycardia, Bradycardia, and Bundle Branch Block

questions.stem: The mechanism for the increased stroke volume of the beat following a PVC is primarily:
options: Increased preload from the prolonged filling interval, augmenting contraction (Frank–Starling mechanism)
questions.explanation: The compensatory pause extends diastole and filling, so the next sinus beat ejects a larger volume — the "post-PVC beat may increase stroke volume" phenomenon that causes measurement fluctuation.
tags: Rhythm Effects on Echocardiography — AFib, PVCs, Tachycardia, Bradycardia, and Bundle Branch Block

questions.stem: Frequent PVCs affect an echocardiographic study mainly by causing:
options: Fluctuation of functional measurements between cycles
questions.explanation: Beat-to-beat differences in filling and contraction (PVC vs post-PVC vs normal beats) make functional measurements such as stroke volume and ejection fraction fluctuate unless averaged.
tags: Rhythm Effects on Echocardiography — AFib, PVCs, Tachycardia, Bradycardia, and Bundle Branch Block

questions.stem: The principal mechanical consequence of tachycardia relevant to echocardiography is:
questions.explanation: As heart rate increases, diastole shortens disproportionately, reducing filling time. This alters Doppler filling patterns and complicates both image acquisition and interpretation.
tags: Rhythm Effects on Echocardiography — AFib, PVCs, Tachycardia, Bradycardia, and Bundle Branch Block

questions.stem: Bradycardia is clinically significant during echocardiography because severe slowing may:
options: Reduce cardiac output despite increased stroke volume
questions.explanation: Although each beat fills more completely, a rate that is too low cannot maintain cardiac output (CO = HR × SV). The lecture notes bradycardia may reduce cardiac output.
tags: Rhythm Effects on Echocardiography — AFib, PVCs, Tachycardia, Bradycardia, and Bundle Branch Block

questions.stem: Rapid heart rates complicate echocardiographic image acquisition primarily because:
options: The ECG cannot be recorded simultaneously
There is less time per cycle to sample and frames per phase become fewer
The transducer must be removed during tachycardia
questions.explanation: At high rates, each cardiac phase lasts only a few frames, making freezing at end-diastole or end-systole and interpreting Doppler considerably more difficult.
tags: Rhythm Effects on Echocardiography — AFib, PVCs, Tachycardia, Bradycardia, and Bundle Branch Block

questions.stem: The fundamental electrical abnormality in bundle branch block is:
options: Delayed activation of the ventricle served by the blocked branch
questions.explanation: With one bundle branch blocked, the affected ventricle is activated late by spread from the other ventricle, producing dyssynchronous contraction and a wide QRS.
tags: Rhythm Effects on Echocardiography — AFib, PVCs, Tachycardia, Bradycardia, and Bundle Branch Block

questions.stem: In left bundle branch block, the echocardiographer should anticipate:
options: Abnormal septal motion due to dyssynchronous ventricular activation
A narrow QRS on the ECG
questions.explanation: Delayed left ventricular activation makes the septum move abnormally (paradoxically), alters ventricular measurements, and may cause ejection fraction estimates to vary.
tags: Rhythm Effects on Echocardiography — AFib, PVCs, Tachycardia, Bradycardia, and Bundle Branch Block

questions.stem: Ventricular dyssynchrony from bundle branch block affects echocardiographic assessment by:
options: Altering ventricular measurements and potentially causing ejection fraction estimates to vary
questions.explanation: Because the ventricles contract at different times, dimensional and volumetric measurements at any single phase may not represent true global function, reducing measurement reliability.
tags: Rhythm Effects on Echocardiography — AFib, PVCs, Tachycardia, Bradycardia, and Bundle Branch Block

questions.stem: On the ECG, a complete bundle branch block is recognized by a QRS duration of:
options: Greater than or equal to 0.12 second with an abnormal contour
questions.explanation: Slowed cell-to-cell conduction beyond the block prolongs ventricular activation time to ≥0.12 s, and the QRS contour becomes abnormal (notched or slurred).
tags: Rhythm Effects on Echocardiography — AFib, PVCs, Tachycardia, Bradycardia, and Bundle Branch Block

questions.stem: Right bundle branch block (RBBB) causes which echocardiographic consequence?
options: Loss of the Doppler A wave
Immediate reduction in ejection fraction to zero
Delayed right ventricular activation with possible paradoxical septal motion
questions.explanation: The right ventricle depolarizes late via the left ventricle, so RV contraction is delayed and septal motion may appear abnormal on echo — a pitfall in interpreting RV and septal measurements.
tags: Rhythm Effects on Echocardiography — AFib, PVCs, Tachycardia, Bradycardia, and Bundle Branch Block

questions.stem: Which patient rhythm most urgently requires the sonographer to average Doppler and dimensional measurements over several beats?
options: Atrial fibrillation with an irregularly irregular ventricular response
Sinus bradycardia with a regular 55 bpm
Sinus rhythm with occasional uniform PACs
questions.explanation: The irregularly irregular rhythm of AFib produces the greatest beat-to-beat variability in filling, stroke volume, and Doppler velocities, making multi-beat averaging essential.
tags: Rhythm Effects on Echocardiography — AFib, PVCs, Tachycardia, Bradycardia, and Bundle Branch Block

questions.stem: In a patient with marked sinus tachycardia, transmitral Doppler E and A waves may be difficult to distinguish because:
options: The A wave disappears with any fast heart rate
Diastole is so short that E and A waves fuse together
Doppler cannot record at fast rates
The E wave equals the stroke volume
questions.explanation: At rapid rates, diastole shortens dramatically, causing the early (E) and atrial (A) filling waves to merge into a single wave — one of several reasons Doppler interpretation becomes more difficult.
tags: Rhythm Effects on Echocardiography — AFib, PVCs, Tachycardia, Bradycardia, and Bundle Branch Block

questions.stem: During an echocardiographic study of a patient with frequent PVCs, the most defensible measurement practice is to:
options: Measure sinus (non-PVC) beats and average several beats, excluding the PVC and noting the post-PVC beat's variability
Report the first measurement regardless of beat type
Stop the study because PVCs always make measurements invalid
questions.explanation: Sinus beats represent the patient's baseline function; PVC and immediate post-PVC beats have abnormal filling and contractility, so they should be excluded or averaged cautiously.
tags: Rhythm Effects on Echocardiography — AFib, PVCs, Tachycardia, Bradycardia, and Bundle Branch Block

questions.stem: The overarching principle connecting all rhythm effects on echo is that:
options: Mechanical function follows electrical activity, so any rhythm disturbance alters the mechanical cycle being measured
Electrical activity is irrelevant to echo measurements
Only wide QRS rhythms affect Doppler
Echo measurements are immune to rhythm variation
questions.explanation: "Mechanical function follows electrical activity": every rhythm disturbance (irregularity, rate change, dyssynchrony) changes filling, contraction timing, or coordination — and therefore the measurements. ---
tags: Sonographer Practice, Patient Safety, and Integration

questions.stem: Throughout the echocardiographic examination, the sonographer should:
options: Turn off the ECG to reduce clutter
Record the ECG only at the end of the study
Rely on the patient's pulse by touch instead of the ECG
questions.explanation: Continuous ECG monitoring is standard practice: it provides real-time rhythm information, supports timing, and allows recognition of rhythms that affect image quality and patient safety.
tags: Sonographer Practice, Patient Safety, and Integration

questions.stem: If the patient becomes unstable during the echocardiographic examination, the correct action is to:
options: Stop the examination, ensure patient safety, and notify the supervisor or responsible clinician
Continue imaging until the full protocol is complete
Leave the room and continue later without telling anyone
Increase the transducer pressure to improve images
questions.explanation: Patient safety takes priority over completing the study. The lecture directs the sonographer to prioritize safety and notify the supervisor if the patient is unstable.
tags: Sonographer Practice, Patient Safety, and Integration

questions.stem: During an irregular rhythm, chamber and Doppler measurements should be:
options: Taken from one beat and reported as definitive
questions.explanation: Because stroke volume and filling vary from beat to beat in irregular rhythms, averaging measurements improves accuracy and reproducibility.
tags: Sonographer Practice, Patient Safety, and Integration

questions.stem: Recognizing rhythms that affect image quality is important to the sonographer because:
options: It replaces the need for an interpreting physician
The ECG determines the transducer frequency
It allows the exam to be stopped for any PAC
It guides how images are acquired, how measurements are averaged, and when findings need attention
questions.explanation: The sonographer's stated responsibilities include recognizing rhythms affecting image quality, adjusting measurement strategy accordingly, and communicating clinically significant findings.
tags: Sonographer Practice, Patient Safety, and Integration

questions.stem: Which principle should guide the sonographer's conduct throughout the examination?
options: Completing the study takes priority over the patient's condition
The ECG can be ignored if images look adequate
Rhythm changes during a study are never important
Patient safety is the priority during examinations
questions.explanation: The lecture's explicit guidance: prioritize patient safety during examinations — including responding to instability or concerning rhythm changes rather than pushing on with imaging.
tags: Sonographer Practice, Patient Safety, and Integration

questions.stem: Which finding during an echocardiographic study most clearly warrants pausing the examination and alerting the supervising clinician?
options: A consistent heart rate of 78 bpm throughout
One isolated PAC in an otherwise normal tracing
New sustained chest discomfort with hypotension and a rapidly changing rhythm
